The expanding universe

Expansion & geometryCosmic chronologyOrigin of matterEvidence & uncertaintiesReading the reference imageSimulation modelReferences

Expansion is a change in distances throughout space

The hot Big Bang describes an earlier, hotter, denser universe. It does not describe matter detonating at a point inside a pre-existing empty arena. In a homogeneous model, widely separated observers participate in the same expansion. Their local coordinate origins are interchangeable; neither is the location where the universe began. A finite picture can represent only a selected region, not the totality of space. [1]

Write a galaxy's ideal comoving position as x and the scale factor as a(t). Its physical separation from another comoving galaxy is d(t) = a(t)|x₂ − x₁|. Moving the coordinate origin cancels in this difference. Differentiating gives v = H(t)d, with H = ȧ/a. This is why recession increases with separation from every comoving observer. There is no need for an exterior space into which the universe expands. [1]

d(t) = a(t) Δχ   ·   H(t) = ȧ/a   ·   v = Hd   ·   1 + z = 1/a

These statements apply to the average cosmic flow. Bound structures have their own dynamics: atoms, planets, stars, galaxies and many groups do not simply grow with the scale factor. Nearby galaxies may approach each other. Homogeneity and isotropy are large-scale statistical approximations, not claims that every region is identical or every pair of objects recedes. [2]

The observable universe is an observer-dependent region limited by the travel of signals through cosmic history. Its horizon is not a wall. Recession speed in cosmological coordinates is distinct from a locally measured relative velocity. [29] Whether the whole universe is finite or infinite remains unresolved; local near-flatness does not uniquely determine global topology. A spherical observation region can therefore coexist with a universe having no preferred center. The simulation's circular mask is simply a viewing window. [2]

From the earliest limits to the present

The following dates are approximate physical landmarks. Epochs overlap and transitions take time. The age of approximately 13.8 billion years is inferred within cosmological models; it is not a directly recorded stopwatch reading. A Planck-like baseline is useful and well constrained, but its fitted parameters are conditional on assumptions. [3]

Inflation is not an observed first frame

Inflation proposes an early interval of accelerated expansion. It offers an explanation for large-scale smoothness, near-flatness and the origin of primordial perturbations. Its success as an organizing framework does not establish a particular inflationary field or a unique energy scale. Reheating is the proposed transfer into a hot bath after inflation. Playback uses an arbitrary internal anchor for this chapter; the interface does not present it as an established date. [4]

Cooling changes what can survive

A high-temperature bath continually creates, scatters and destroys particles. As it cools, the accessible species and reaction rates change. CERN studies quark–gluon matter experimentally with heavy-ion collisions, providing a laboratory connection to early-universe conditions. This does not recreate the expansion of the universe itself. There is no scientifically justified ordered list in which one familiar chemical substance was created before all fundamental particles. [5]

Matter and antimatter annihilate efficiently, yet a small net matter excess survives. Explaining the origin of that asymmetry remains a central problem. Laboratory measurements of particle–antiparticle differences constrain the possibilities; they do not by themselves settle cosmic baryogenesis. A visualization should therefore show the surviving inventory without inventing its cause. [11]

Light nuclei precede neutral atoms

Once deuterium can resist photodissociation, reactions incorporate many surviving neutrons into helium-4. The early result is roughly three parts hydrogen to one part helium by ordinary-matter mass, plus trace light isotopes. There is no substantial primordial production of carbon, oxygen or iron. The lithium discrepancy between standard predictions and old metal-poor stars remains unresolved. These successes and tensions make nucleosynthesis a test, not merely a historical story. [6]

Hydrogen recombination later reduces free-electron scattering, allowing pre-existing thermal photons to travel much farther. Helium becomes neutral earlier. The word “recombination” is conventional even though much hydrogen is becoming neutral for the first time. The present 2.7 K glow is redshifted radiation from a much hotter epoch, not light freshly emitted by every new atom. The plasma-to-transparent transition is extended; it is not a sudden universal switch. [7]

Precision recombination calculations include excited atomic levels and radiation transport. The simple p + e⁻ → H + γ schematic is not a calculation of the cosmological ionization history. [20]

Structure forms while the background expands

Density perturbations grow under gravity. Dark matter supplies potential wells; gas cooling lets baryons collapse much further. The earliest stars form locally, not simultaneously everywhere. Their ultraviolet output ionizes surrounding gas and growing populations eventually transform much of the intergalactic medium. The first-star population remains uncertain, and evidence for late reionization extends to roughly 1.1 billion years in one quasar-sightline analysis. A reionization midpoint is not the date of the very first star. [21] [22] Likewise, a newly detected early galaxy gives an observational bound, not the birth certificate of all galaxies. [8] [9]

How the material inventory grows

Cosmic chemical evolution is a network. Hydrogen can become stellar helium; helium burning supplies carbon; advanced burning and explosions produce additional nuclei. Material can stay locked inside a remnant, escape into interstellar gas, condense into dust, join another star, or become part of a planet. These are different physical processes: nucleosynthesis changes nuclei, ionization changes electron binding, chemistry rearranges atoms, and condensation changes material phase. [12]

FamilyMain pathwaysImportant qualification
Hydrogen, helium, trace lithiumBig Bang plus later stellar contributionsPrimordial nuclei and neutral atoms have different formation epochs. [6]
Lithium, beryllium, boronCosmic-ray fragmentation; other sources contributeOrigins depend on isotope, and lithium has stellar contributions. [13]
Carbon through iron-group regionStellar burning and explosive nucleosynthesisMassive stars, evolved stars and Type Ia explosions have different yields. [12,13]
Many nuclei beyond ironSlow and rapid neutron captureOne element can mix multiple isotope-specific pathways. [12,13]
Short-lived and superheavy nucleiRadioactive chains and laboratory production; some cosmic transientsA named element need not have a substantial cosmic abundance. [13,15]
Molecules, grains, rocks and iceChemistry, cooling, condensation and assemblyThese are combinations or phases of existing elements. [10]

Neutron-star mergers provide a concrete observational link to neutron-rich nucleosynthesis. The identification of strontium in the kilonova associated with GW170817 connected a neutron-capture element to such an event. This is strong evidence for an r-process site; it does not show that all gold, or every heavy element, came exclusively from mergers. Other sites and the relative contributions remain active research topics. [14]

The element atlas includes the 118 named elements, but uses broad pathway families rather than fabricated percentages. A universally precise first-production timestamp does not exist for each entry. The earliest production, local enrichment, solar abundance and current terrestrial inventory are different questions. Journal reviews describe overlapping production sites and isotope-dependent pathways; the atlas is a broad orientation, not an isotope abundance database. [23] [24] The NASA origin chart is a useful richer map of overlapping contributions, while IUPAC supplies the authoritative element nomenclature. [13] [15]

About 4.6 billion years ago, the material that became our Solar System condensed from an enriched molecular cloud into a disk around a forming star. Solid grains accumulated into larger bodies. The ingredients inherited previous generations of nuclear processing. Earth's existence is therefore much later than the origin of its hydrogen, and its constituent heavier nuclei need not share a single stellar ancestor. [10]

Evidence, model dependence and open questions

Scientific review: 10 September 2026. The broad history follows established cosmology; numerical parameters are model dependent and the animations are schematic. Journal publication does not make every interpretation settled consensus. The references distinguish published research, expert reviews, educational resources and a recent preprint.

The case for a hot expanding past comes from mutually consistent observations: recession and distance relations, a nearly thermal microwave background, primordial light-element abundances and the development of large-scale structure. The Planck analysis fits a compact ΛCDM model to detailed CMB measurements, inferring quantities such as expansion rate, matter density and age. Its baseline H₀ is about 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and total matter fraction about 0.315. Other probes test this reconstruction; agreement must not be assumed in advance. [3]

Newer CMB measurements do not define one universally agreed replacement for H₀. ACT DR6 reports 68.43 ± 0.27 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ for its specified Planck–ACT, lensing and DESI DR2 combination within ΛCDM. Our retained 67.4 value is the documented Planck baseline, not a claim to be a fresh combined-data fit. [19]

Ordinary matter is only a small part of the present cosmic energy budget. Common rounded summaries give about 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter and 68% dark energy. Dark matter is inferred through gravity, while dark energy describes the component associated with late acceleration. Neither has a settled microscopic identity. Neither is a chemical element. Their percentages also evolve with cosmic time. [16]

Constant dark energy is a baseline assumption, not a guarantee about eternity. Published DESI DR2 results find that BAO alone is well described by flat ΛCDM; combinations with CMB and supernova data favor evolving dark energy to differing degrees. This is an active challenge, not an established replacement model. The July 2026 Lyα analysis is a separate preprint; its journal publication was not established at this review date. This application retains its explicit constant-Λ baseline. [17] [18]

Unresolved questions include the microscopic origin of inflation, the matter excess, the identities of dark matter and dark energy, the lithium discrepancy, the detailed first-star population and the global extent of space. Nothing in this simulation establishes what came “before,” why the laws exist, or whether expansion will continue forever.

Reading the reference image critically

The supplied illustration is visually useful as an all-directions expansion concept. Its captions mix supported physical ideas with stronger philosophical or speculative assertions. It should not be treated as a source of measurements.

Image claimScientifically defensible reading
Expansion from every pointA useful description of the ideal large-scale flow, with no preferred comoving origin. [1]
Every point moves away from every otherApplies to ideal unbound comoving separations, not all bound structures or peculiar motions. [2]
No edge; endless expansionNo observed physical boundary is established. Infinite extent and eternal expansion are not measured facts. [2,17]
Before the beginning there was nothingNo empirical cosmological result establishes this assertion. The earliest regime is unresolved. [4]
All matter, time and laws emerged togetherThe hot Big Bang does not establish the ultimate origin of laws or time. Familiar structures and elements formed at different epochs.
Stars and galaxies are only a resultThey form within the expanding universe, but matter and radiation also enter gravitational dynamics. Expansion alone does not make galaxies.
“UniversalExpand” is a fundamental modelIt is used here as the project name. The scientific background model is explicitly ΛCDM.

What the simulation actually computes

The application has three distinct levels. The cosmic scene is an illustrative 3D reconstruction. The expansion laboratory applies the homogeneous distance law exactly to a small coordinate set. The numerical background integrates a specified Friedmann model. These levels share an educational purpose but do not have identical fidelity.

Numerical background

H(a) = H₀ √(Ωr a⁻⁴ + Ωm a⁻³ + ΩΛ)
t(a) = ∫ da / [a H(a)]
Tγ(a) = 2.7255 K / a

The parameters are H₀ = 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, Ωm = 0.315, Ωr = 0.000092 and ΩΛ = 0.684908. Curvature is zero. The integrator uses 8,000 logarithmic intervals from a = 10⁻¹² to 1, a radiation-era initial estimate, and trapezoidal integration in ln(a). Logarithmic interpolation then supplies a at a requested age. This configuration yields about 13.791 billion years at a = 1 and approximately 2,932 K at 380,000 years. The final chapter uses the conventional rounded 13.8-billion-year label and clamps a to 1. Displayed decimal places describe deterministic model output, not observational error bars. The adopted present CMB temperature follows the measured value rounded to 2.7255 K. [25]

Ωm includes ordinary and dark matter. The radiation term approximates a fixed effective relativistic-neutrino contribution; a precision treatment would evolve neutrino masses and species-dependent thermal histories. The simulation therefore reports a, z and the radiation temperature only from recombination onward. Earlier chapter temperatures are approximate landmarks, not outputs of a nuclear or particle-transport solver. At 10⁻¹² seconds, the radiation-dominated Standard Model estimate t(s) T(MeV)² ≈ 2.4/√g*, with g* = 106.75, gives about 6 × 10¹⁵ K. Changes in particle content and entropy transfer prevent extrapolating the fixed late-time radiation term through the entire early history. [1]

Visual reconstruction and time controls

The cosmic scene draws 13,720 tracer sprites at genuine three-dimensional positions. Galaxy centers come from a seeded, jittered lattice, with illustrative local particle distributions. Before structure formation the sample is diffuse. A smooth interpolation assembles clusters from the dark-ages chapters onward. This is not an N-body or hydrodynamical calculation and the particles are not a measured galaxy catalog.

The visual expansion factor is 0.65 + 0.16 × chapter position. This deliberately compresses the enormous physical dynamic range, while applying the same factor in x, y and z. In the mature scene, local galaxy offsets are kept fixed as intergalactic centers separate, illustrating that bound structures do not swell. Finite sample boundaries and the circular crop are rendering limits, not cosmic edges. Colors and apparent particle sizes carry explanatory meaning, not spectroscopy.

The twelve chapter landmarks are equally spaced around a partial circle; adjacent internal times interpolate logarithmically. The quantum-frontier and inflation chapters have arbitrary internal timing anchors for playback, not measured dates; their age readouts explicitly withhold an event time. Playback spends comparable time between milestones despite vastly different physical durations. This makes the first seconds and the last billions of years both inspectable. It must not be interpreted as a constant-rate clock. The scene is a cosmic-time slice, not an observer's past light cone; it does not ray-trace light propagation, lensing or redshift.

Expansion and reaction demonstrations

The expansion laboratory uses seven fixed 3D comoving points. Distances are multiplied by an adjustable relative factor from 1 to 3. Its tabulated recession velocities use a fixed H₀ for a controlled comparison; changing this factor is not advancing a self-consistent cosmological solution. Subtracting the selected observer's position changes the origin without changing pairwise separations.

The particle-process view animates selected reaction schematics: quark confinement, deuterium assembly, radiative recombination and triple-alpha burning. Motion, geometry and speed are illustrative. Bound nucleons and electron clouds are symbols, not measured quantum trajectories. The cloud represents one electron; its radial sampling is illustrative and is not a calculated hydrogen wavefunction. Atomic radiative recombination must not be confused with weak nuclear electron capture. Quantum wavefunctions, reaction probabilities, cross-sections, energy spectra and nuclear yields are not simulated. The triple-alpha animation compresses its intermediate beryllium-8 stage. Reaction playback has its own progress control and does not advance cosmic time.

A fully predictive multiscale universe calculation would require general-relativistic background evolution, perturbation transfer functions, gravity, gas dynamics, radiative transfer, chemical and nuclear networks, stellar evolution and sub-resolution prescriptions. No finite desktop visualization can resolve every particle, every material phase and the whole universe over all scales. This project provides an inspectable educational representation with explicit boundaries instead of claiming that capability.
